implementation_notes: EF Core's DbContext is the write-behind unit of work: every queried or attached entity is tracked, property-level changes are recorded in memory, and SQL is generated only when SaveChangesAsync is called, which wraps the whole change set in a single transaction and emits one UPDATE per changed row even if the property was modified repeatedly. Keep the context request-scoped (the docs call it a short-lived unit of work) and call SaveChanges at the boundary you choose.
pitfalls: A long-lived DbContext grows the change set without bound and serves stale tracked entities - treat it as a unit of work and dispose it.
Untracked queries (AsNoTracking) return entities whose changes SaveChanges will not see; mixing the two silently drops writes.
SaveChanges is transactional per call, not per request: multi-step work outside one call can commit partially.

variants.name: Bounded Channel + BackgroundService flusher
variants.idiom_name: System.Threading.Channels bounded queue + IHostedService flush loop
variants.implementation_notes: When the store has no change-tracked context (Dapper, raw ADO.NET, or batches that must span requests), build the queue instead: a bounded System.Threading.Channels.Channel<Change> fed by handlers and drained by a BackgroundService, which groups the drained batch by table and writes it in one transaction per group. The channel replaces the hand-rolled buffer and provides the back-pressure decision through BoundedChannelFullMode.
pitfalls: Choosing DropWrite/DropOldest as the overflow mode is silent data loss - decide block/reject/spill explicitly and surface the policy.
StopAsync must drain the channel before exiting, or queued changes are abandoned at shutdown.
Grouping by table is not enough for referential order: inserts must precede foreign-key dependents in the same batch.
